facts.claim: "Cast Iron Heart" is a duet between Emily Scott Robinson and John Paul White, from her album Appalachia, released January 30, 2026 on Oh Boy Records.
Robinson says she wrote the song as a celebration of love that has been changed by aging and loss, in contrast to the many love songs about young, untested love.
Robinson says John Paul White's voice has depth and gravitas.
Appalachia was produced by Josh Kaufman, whose credits include Grateful Dead, Anaïs Mitchell and Bonny Light Horseman. It was recorded at Dreamland Recording Studios in upstate New York.

The album's credits list the studios as Dreamland Recording Studios, The Isokon and Little Pink, with mixing and mastering by D. James Goodwin. The musicians named are Josh Kaufman, Dunkan Wickel, Annie Nero, Lizzy Ross, Otto Hauser and Harmonica Jerry. The credits do not say which musicians play on this track.
"Cast Iron Heart" was the focus track for Appalachia.
The official video for "Cast Iron Heart" was released alongside the album and was filmed in Florence, Alabama, at White's studio.
Americana UK describes the song as a duet about two people who have been scarred but still choose each other, showing love in maturity after mistakes and heartbreak.

Appalachia is Robinson's third release on Oh Boy Records and her fifth album overall. Her earlier albums Traveling Mercies (2019) and American Siren (2021) appeared on Rolling Stone's best country and Americana lists.

Robinson's 2020 release "The Time for Flowers", recorded at home during the pandemic, caught the attention of Oh Boy Records, the independent label John Prine founded in 1981. She studied at Furman University, moved to Colorado to work as a social worker, and at 26 attended a songwriting retreat that led her to become a performer.

research.lineage: The song sits in contemporary folk and Americana storytelling, shaped by Robinson's Blue Ridge and North Carolina bluegrass and folk roots and by the John Prine-founded Oh Boy Records.

draft:
In **Cast Iron Heart**, the whole argument rides on a skillet. Left out in the rain, rusted, written off, it comes back with a little love and shines like new. Anyone who has kept cast iron knows the rest: it gets better with use, and the black finish is just years of cooking baked in. Emily Scott Robinson builds a love song on that fact, and she never strains the metaphor. "Got a lot of salt and seasoning," goes one line, and it works both ways at once. It is skillet care, and it is a person admitting they've been through things.

Robinson has said she wrote it to celebrate love that aging and loss have changed, a pushback against all the songs about young love that hasn't been tested yet. You can hear the pushback in the lyric. "People think we're past our prime" gets answered right away with the claim that they arrived just in time. That's pride, and a little defiance. But the bridge drops the guard: live long enough and your heart breaks a thousand times, so why do it alone? The song offers companionship the way someone offers it after they've learned what being alone costs.

The tenderness is in the chores. There's coffee made strong at dawn, butter in the pan, a kiss for calloused hands. Then comes the most loving line in the song, a detail most love songs would edit out: "The lines around your hazel eyes." Wrinkles get praised alongside a magnolia bloom. The song doesn't flinch from age. It looks right at it.

Robinson doesn't settle every doubt, and that's to her credit. "Maybe we're a vestige of the past," she sings, and then, "Maybe we're just built to last." Both maybes stay on the table. The chorus, a love that deepens as every season comes back around, keeps repeating like a vow said until it holds. The song ends on its first verse too, rust and all, coming back around itself.

The sound stays out of the way. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through slow arpeggios. Brushed drums and a simple bass line keep a relaxed sway, and the room sounds natural and close. The lead voice is slightly nasal and conversational, with a shade of melancholy. A second voice settles in beside it in harmony. Robinson has said John Paul White's voice carries depth and gravitas, and the pairing does what a duet like this needs: two weathered people singing the same promise. Josh Kaufman, whose work with Bonny Light Horseman and Anaïs Mitchell favors this kind of unfussy warmth, produced the album. It's a fitting focus track for a record on the label John Prine founded.

It makes you look at the scuffed, used-up things in your own life, a pan or a face, and see the years of care in them instead of the damage.
